title: GLAD deforestation alert subscriptions reduce deforestation probability in Africa by 18%
summary: Independent evaluation: subscriptions to GLAD Landsat alerts (bagged decision trees) cut deforestation probability in Africa by 18%.
account: Global Forest Watch's GLAD deforestation alerts are produced by the University of Maryland from Landsat imagery using a set of bagged decision trees that estimate per-pixel likelihood of forest loss; the method was published on 2 March 2016. Moffette, Alix-Garcia, Shea and Pickens evaluated the alerts' effect in Nature Climate Change on 4 January 2021, analyzing subscriptions to alerts across 22 tropical countries. They found that subscriptions decreased the probability of deforestation in Africa by 18 percent relative to 2011–2016 baseline levels, with stronger effects in protected areas and concessions, no detectable effect on other continents, and little effect where alerts existed without subscribers; they valued the avoided emissions at USD 149–696 million. The date given is the publication date.
purpose: Detect humid tropical forest disturbance in near real time from Landsat imagery to support land management and enforcement.
system: GLAD (Global Land Analysis and Discovery) Landsat deforestation alerts on Global Forest Watch
developer: University of Maryland GLAD laboratory (Hansen et al.)
deployer: World Resources Institute (Global Forest Watch) and alert subscribers

ratings.reason: General benefit without an event: aggregate statistical effect across subscribed areas, no discrete attributable event.
General benefit without an event: effect measured at the level of subscribed administrative areas and concessions.
General benefit without an event: continent-level reduction estimate with no single identifiable beneficiary.

ai_role.statement: The alerts are a machine-learning product (bagged decision trees) and the evaluation attributes the 18 percent reduction to subscriptions to those alerts rather than to their mere availability; the evaluation's lead authors are independent economists, but co-authors are from WRI (operator) and the University of Maryland (producer).

paired_incident.title: Government‑Backed AI4Peat Mapping Tool Allegedly Misidentifies Granite Outcrops and Quarries as Peat
paired_incident.basis: Natural England's ML land-cover mapping from imagery misclassified granite and quarries as peat, misdirecting conservation; GLAD's Landsat classifier maps forest loss for the same users.

headline: GLAD alerts cut deforestation probability in Africa by 18%
metric: decreased the probability of deforestation in Africa by 18 percent

comparator.against: average 2011–2016 deforestation levels, with areas lacking alert subscribers as the counterfactual across 22 tropical countries
comparator.after: probability of deforestation in Africa decreased by 18%; no effect on other continents
comparator.quote: Here, we show that subscriptions to alerts in 22 tropical countries decrease the probability of deforestation in Africa by 18% relative to the average 2011–2016 levels. There is no effect on other continents, and the availability of alerts does not significantly change deforestation outcomes.

later.note: Global Forest Watch kept the Landsat-based GLAD alerts (GLAD-L) running and in 2022 folded them into an integrated disturbance alerts layer with GLAD-S2, RADD and, from January 2026, DIST-ALERT.
later.quote: GLAD-L is GFW's longest-standing alert product from the UMD Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) lab and uses imagery from NASA's Landsat satellites to detect tree cover loss at 30-meter resolution.

value.amount: between US$149 million and US$696 million
value.what: value of avoided deforestation in Africa, priced at the social cost of carbon
value.quote: Calculated using the social cost of carbon for avoided deforestation in Africa, we estimate the alert system’s value to be between US$149 million and US$696 million.
